newsitem.title: UK: Germany caught in home-made 'euro trap' -economist.
newsitem.headline: Germany caught in home-made 'euro trap' -economist.

text.p: The German government is caught in a "euro trap" of its own making, which could ultimately force European monetary union to be delayed, Juergen von Hagen, economics professor at Bonn University, said.

He said the government had assured the German public that the only possible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU) was a strict, literal one, which would ensure the euro common currency was as strong as the mark.
However, Germany itself now risked missing the EMU deficit goal of three percent to GDP, which would rob it of the clout to exclude states such as Italy on the same basis, he said.

"Germany will not make the three percent deficit criterion. That's for sure already," Von Hagen, who is also a research fellow at the Centre for Economic Policy Research, told a meeting organised by the CEPR in London.
Members of the Bundesbank council have already cast doubt on whether Germany can meet the three percent deficit goal, but argue that EMU must begin as planned on January 1, 1999.
Should Germany miss the EMU targets but France hit them, they and a broad grouping including such states as Spain, Italy and Portugal were likely to begin EMU in 1999, said Von Hagen.
That, however, could cost German Chancellor Helmut Kohl the next election as the already widespread hostility to monetary union among the German public increased, he argued.
A second likely scenario had both lynchpins, Germany and France, declaring they were not ready for EMU and that the only option was to postpone the launch for three or four years.
That, however, would tempt those governments to loosen fiscal policy, leading to significant exchange rate adjustments and, in turn, a yet longer postponement of EMU, Von Hagen said.
"The German government has manoeuvred itself into what I would describe as a 'euro trap'," he said.
